title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
text: For the next two decades, the U.S. power system will rest on three pillars: renewables, nuclear and natural gas. The more useful way to say it is that the system needs three jobs done (cheap energy, firm capacity and flexibility), and each fuel is good at some of them. Gas will lose weight over that period, but it will remain a pillar until at least 2050. And in this decade the scarcest job is not cheap energy but firm capacity that can actually connect to the grid.

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
text:
Three jobs, not three fuels
Today these three pillars already carry the system: in 2025, gas supplied about 41% of U.S. utility-scale generation, nuclear about 18%, wind about 11% and solar about 7% (EIA). Listing fuels, though, hides what each one is for.

Cheap energy. Wind and solar produce the cheapest megawatt-hours when they run, and they dominate what is being built: of the 86 GW planned for 2026, solar and batteries make up nearly 80% (EIA). I count geothermal here too. The first next-generation geothermal units only began commercial operation this year (Fervo), so its contribution is still ahead of us.
Firm capacity. Nuclear and gas run when the weather does not cooperate and when a large load needs power around the clock.
Flexibility. Batteries, hydrogen and flexible demand move energy in time. In my own work, hydrogen earned its place as a flexibility tool, not as a fourth pillar: in Texas, renewable hydrogen covered only a small share of industrial demand (International Journal of Hydrogen Energy, 2025), while at nuclear plants its value came from turning baseload output into a flexible product (Nature Communications, 2026).

I leave fusion out of this picture. It may matter later, but it will not shape planning decisions made this decade.

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
section: Gas: still a pillar, with less weight
text:
Gas: still a pillar, with less weight
The Energy Information Administration’s 2026 outlook projects that gas, solar and wind together supply about 80% of U.S. generation by 2050 in most of its cases (EIA, April 2026). I read that as confirmation that gas stays a pillar for the next two decades. I expect its weight to shrink, and its role to move from bulk energy toward firm capacity that backs up renewables and large new loads.
What no longer holds is the planning habit of assuming that a gas plant can appear whenever a model wants it. GE Vernova reports 122 GW of gas-turbine backlog and slot reservations, has sold delivery slots into 2032, and prices 2026 orders roughly 50% higher per kilowatt than 2025 orders (GE Vernova, Q3 2026). The supply chain is not broken, so the assumption still holds in part. But a turbine slot is now a constraint with a date on it.

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
section: Why now: the scarce job is firm capacity that can connect
text:
Why now: the scarce job is firm capacity that can connect
Data centers used about 4.7% of U.S. electricity in 2024, and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s reference case reaches 11.8% by 2030 (LBNL, 2025 update). That demand arrives faster than the grid can absorb it:

Projects that reached operation in 2025 spent a median of more than five years in interconnection queues, and only 13% of the capacity that requested interconnection from 2000 to 2020 was built (LBNL Queued Up).
The country built 322 miles of new high-voltage (345 kV and above) transmission in 2024 (Grid Strategies and ACEG).
PJM’s 2028/29 capacity auction cleared at its price cap and still fell about 6.8 GW short of its reliability requirement (PJM).

When connection is the bottleneck, waiting becomes a cost in its own right. In my work on delayed grid energization, the cost to the developer of a 300 MW (IT) data center waiting 36 months ran to the order of $0.7 billion in present value, and who ends up paying depended on how large-load tariffs are designed (CoDE framework).

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
section: The nuclear pillar starts with the plants we already have
text:
The nuclear pillar starts with the plants we already have
The fastest firm, carbon-free megawatts are often the ones already built. In a study of 42 U.S. reactors at 2024 prices, nearly all had negative net present value when run as baseload plants; adding hydrogen production and grid services, with the assumed hydrogen credit, brought most of them above zero (Nature Communications, 2026). The same logic shows up in today’s news: DOE has offered up to $5 billion for uprates that add about 1.1 GW at eight existing plants (DOE), and retired reactors are being prepared for restart. New reactors are a different decision: for a reactor serving a hyperscale data center, I found that capital cost and policy, far more than operating choices, decide whether it beats grid supply (Energy Conversion and Management, accepted).

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
section: Policy should pay for the service, not for one output
text:
Policy should pay for the service, not for one output
If the system needs three jobs, incentives should pay for the job a plant does. Today’s main clean-electricity credit pays per megawatt-hour generated. In the same data-center study, that design made it more expensive to use reactor steam for cooling, because every unit of steam sent to the chiller forgoes both electricity and its credit; an incentive meant to close a capital gap ends up discouraging the more efficient use of the plant. The tax law also treats the three jobs unevenly: wind and solar lose the main credits for projects placed in service after 2027 unless construction began by July 4, 2026, while nuclear, geothermal and storage keep them into the next decade (26 U.S.C. § 45Y). Paying for delivered services (energy, firm capacity, flexibility, and heat or cooling where it is used) would let each pillar compete for the job it does best.

title: Three Pillars, Three Jobs: How Renewables, Nuclear and Gas Will Share the U.S. Power System
text:
What would change my mind

If gas-turbine delivery times fall back to about three years and gas’s share falls much faster than EIA projects, gas is a bridge, not a pillar.
If enhanced geothermal reaches DOE’s cost goal at scale, it belongs among the firm-capacity sources as much as among the cheap-energy ones.
If large loads show verified, measured flexibility in the gigawatts, flexibility becomes a pillar in its own right and the firm-capacity gap shrinks.

title: Data & Tools for Energy-Systems Modeling
text: This guide is for researchers, students and analysts who build models of U.S. power markets, of large new loads such as data centers and electrolyzers, and of the clean firm supply that may serve them. It covers fifteen public datasets and open tools in five groups: grid operations and markets; generation, load and emissions; interconnection and planning; costs and technology; and modeling tools. Each entry says who publishes the source, what it covers, how to get it, what its terms allow (including whether you may redistribute what you download), and the pitfalls that tend to cost time. Where a pitfall comes from my own published work, the entry links the public documentation of the framework repository in which the step is written down; the others come from the publisher’s own documentation. As of 2 November 2026, every fact below was checked against the publisher’s official pages. Terms, versions and addresses change, so confirm them at the source before you rely on them. One naming note: on 1 December 2025 the U.S. Department of Energy changed the name of the lab known as NREL (National Renewable Energy Laboratory); it is now the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR). Its tools and data now live on nlr.gov, and older nrel.gov links no longer resolve.

title: Data & Tools for Energy-Systems Modeling
text:
Grid operations & markets

ERCOT 60-day SCED and DAM disclosure reports
What it is. ERCOT, the grid and market operator for most of Texas, publishes resource-level dispatch, offer and award data once a 60-day confidentiality period has passed. The 60-Day SCED Disclosure Reports (NP3-965-ER) cover real-time security-constrained economic dispatch. The 60-Day DAM Disclosure Reports (NP3-966-ER) cover the day-ahead market.
Coverage. Both reports have run daily since 29 January 2011, with one ZIP package of CSV files per operating day. The SCED package includes separate files for generation resources, load resources and energy storage resources in SCED, at SCED-interval resolution. The DAM package includes energy bids and awards, resource data and ancillary-service offers and awards. ERCOT’s market reports index lists these alongside the shorter 2-day and 3-day disclosures.
Access.

Open the product page and download the daily ZIP files. ERCOT’s Disclosure Reports Column Definitions Guide, linked there, defines the columns.
For long histories, use the ERCOT Data Access Portal or the Public API (see the next entry).
Expect a lag of about 60 days. For example, ERCOT’s notices show that the report for operating day 27 June 2024 was posted on 26 August 2024.

License and terms. ERCOT’s Terms of Use let you use, reproduce and redistribute public content on two conditions: the content is not modified, and its copyright and other notices are kept. Raw data may go into your own compilations, charts and analyses without those notices. ERCOT does not warrant the accuracy of the data, and its name and logo need written permission. Redistribution: allowed for unmodified files; derived analyses allowed.
Known pitfalls.

Clock. ERCOT data follow Central Prevailing Time, so every spring has a missing hour and every fall a repeated one. On the long day, ERCOT labels the repeated hour separately from the normal one. My Texas hydrogen framework converts every series to one fixed-offset clock before aggregating, then reindexes it to a complete hourly axis.
From intervals to hours. Average each resource’s SCED intervals within each hour to get its energy for that hour. An hour without a record is missing, not zero. Fill only short gaps, resource by resource, before summing to zones; after summing, a silent resource is hidden by its neighbours.
Locations. Disclosure files identify resources by ERCOT name, not by county. The framework matches each one to its plant in EIA-860, which gives the county and from that the weather zone. The mapping table is kept under version control, and unmatched capacity is reviewed.
Capacity factors. The denominator should be the capacity actually operating in that hour, taken from commissioning dates; year-end capacity understates early-year capacity factors. Look at the maximum before any clipping: a value above 1 means a matching or capacity error.
Corrections. ERCOT sometimes reposts disclosure data. A March 2026 market notice, for example, announced supplemental files for a load-resource file affected from December 2025 to January 2026. Watch the market notices and re-download the affected days.

Used in. Hydrogen’s role in expanding renewable energy in Texas (TXH2). The full recipe and its checks are in the txh2-ercot-hydrogen data pipeline.


ERCOT prices, the Data Access Portal and the Public API
What it is. ERCOT’s public market reports, including prices, are available through three routes: the data-product pages on ercot.com, the ERCOT Data Access Portal for search and archives, and the ERCOT Public API.
Coverage. DAM Settlement Point Prices (NP4-190-CD) give day-ahead prices at resource nodes, load zones and trading hubs. Real-time settlement point prices (NP6-905-CD) are posted every 15 minutes. Bus-level DAM Hourly LMPs (NP4-183-CD) are a separate product. These nodal products have run since late November 2010. The product pages list only recent files; the DAM hourly LMP page, for example, keeps the last 30 days.
Access.

For a quick look, download recent files from the product page.
For history, search the Data Access Portal. Its search reaches back to 30 November 2023; older archives come as downloadable file packages.
For programmatic access, register on the ERCOT API Explorer and subscribe to the Public API product to obtain a subscription key. Then request an ID token with your account credentials; it is valid for one hour and cannot be refreshed. Send both the key and the token with every request, as the registration guide describes. Data through the API start on 11 December 2023.
Open-source clients such as gridstatus (BSD-3-Clause) wrap these steps. My nuclear–data-center framework retrieved ERCOT day-ahead hub prices with it.

License and terms. ERCOT’s API support page states that the same Terms of Use govern the API: unmodified redistribution with notices kept, and free use in your own analyses. Keep your API credentials out of scripts and repositories. Redistribution: as for the disclosure reports.
Known pitfalls.

Settlement point price or LMP. Prices at hubs, load zones and resource nodes, and prices at individual electrical buses, are separate products with separate report IDs. Choose the one for the location your site would face; the nuclear–data-center framework uses the day-ahead price at a hub.
15-minute prices. Average each hour’s intervals before joining them to hourly data. Check that every hour has its full set of intervals, and treat a missing interval as an error, not as a zero.
Negative prices. Keep them. A model that buys and sells at the grid should see hours in which exporting costs money.
Year length. After converting clocks, check that a normal year has exactly 8,760 rows. In a leap year, treat all series alike: remove the leap day from each of them, or keep all 8,784 hours throughout.
Units. Market prices are in $/MWh. Models that work in kW, such as REopt-based ones, need $/kWh, so divide by 1,000.

Used in. Small modular reactor cogeneration for a hyperscale data center, with its smr-datacenter-cogeneration data pipeline; co-located wind and hydrogen, co-located solar and hydrogen and offshore wind–hydrogen O&M, with the reopt-hydrogen-framework data pipeline.


PJM Data Miner
What it is. Data Miner, still called Data Miner 2 on many pages, is PJM Interconnection’s tool for its public market and operations data. It has a web interface and an API.
Coverage. Data are organized as feeds, each with its own definition, posting frequency and retention. Feeds include day-ahead and real-time hourly LMPs, five-minute real-time LMPs, settlement-verified LMPs, hourly load (preliminary, estimated and metered), load forecasts and generation by fuel type. Price feeds cover all bus locations, including aggregates.
Access.

The web interface needs no account. Choose a feed, set the dates, filter, and export to CSV.
For the API, create a PJM account, sign in to the API portal and obtain a key. A non-member must also confirm to PJM by e-mail that the data will be used only for internal business purposes. The steps are in PJM’s Data Miner API Guide.
Every API query needs a date filter, and a standard query is limited to about one year of data.

License and terms. Under the Data Miner terms of use, PJM members may republish data and non-members may not. PJM’s API guide adds that commercial use, including publishing data or making derivatives of it, requires PJM membership (at least Associate Membership). PJM’s API portal states that passing on Data Miner data, or anything derived from it, requires a Redistribution License issued by PJM. Non-members are limited to 6 data connections per minute (members to 600). Redistribution: not allowed without PJM authorization. In practice, publish your code and a download recipe, not the PJM data. The documentation of my supply-chain framework recommends the same approach for any source whose terms forbid redistribution.
Known pitfalls.

Two clocks. Feeds carry both Eastern Prevailing Time (_ept, which observes daylight saving) and UTC (_utc) timestamp columns. PJM recommends filtering and sorting on the same one. Pick one and convert once.
Archive rules. Hourly LMP feeds older than 731 days, and five-minute LMPs older than 186 days, move to an archive. Archive queries must stay within one UTC calendar year, must not span archived and recent data, and allow fewer filters. PJM’s example is that you can request all aggregates by pnode type, but not one specific pnode.
Preliminary and final values. Hourly load comes in preliminary, estimated and metered versions, and LMPs have settlement-verified feeds. State which version you used.
Throughput. At six connections per minute, a non-member’s bulk download of nodal history takes time. Plan it, and keep the raw files with their download dates.

Used in. Hydrogen integration and policy support for U.S. nuclear power plants (NPPH2). PJM is one of the seven U.S. ISO/RTO markets in that study.

title: Data & Tools for Energy-Systems Modeling
text:
Generation, load & emissions

EIA-930 Hourly Electric Grid Monitor
What it is. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) collects hourly operating data from the balancing authorities (BAs) of the Lower 48 states on Form EIA-930. It publishes them through the Hourly Electric Grid Monitor.
Coverage. Hourly data for each BA: demand, demand forecast, net generation, total interchange and interchange with each neighbouring BA. EIA aggregates them into 13 regions and a Lower 48 total. Data start on 1 July 2015. Net generation by energy source, subregion demand and EIA’s estimated CO₂ emissions start on 1 July 2018, and battery storage became a separate energy source on 1 January 2025.
Access. Use the dashboards, the six-month CSV files (balance, interchange and subregion), or the full-history workbooks for each BA and region. The EIA API needs a free registered key and serves EIA-930 data from 1 January 2019 onward; older data are in the downloadable files. EIA’s About the EIA-930 data page is the best single reference.
License and terms. EIA’s copyright and reuse policy places its publications, as federal government works, in the public domain, and lets you use and distribute its data. EIA asks for an acknowledgment that names it and gives the publication date. Redistribution: allowed.
Known pitfalls.

Clock. Values are hour-ending. Each BA reports in a local time zone of its own choosing, and a few choices are unexpected: El Paso Electric reports in Arizona time and Idaho Power in Pacific time, for example. The six-month files carry both a local and a UTC end-of-hour stamp. My carbon-aware load framework works in UTC or local standard time, never in a clock that repeats an hour.
Daylight-saving days. These days have 23 or 25 hours, and EIA notes that they are often misreported, with duplicated, missing or mislabeled hours. Check them before anything else.
Raw, imputed or adjusted. EIA publishes BA-level data as reported, while its regional and national totals include imputation. The six-month files carry raw, imputed and adjusted columns side by side. Choose one deliberately and say which.
Revisions. Values can change after first release. My framework records the access date and a SHA-256 checksum of every downloaded file, so a result can be traced to the exact data used.
Zeros and negatives. An hour with zero demand is a reporting gap and should be treated as missing. My carbon-aware load framework clips negative net generation, such as pumping or station use, to zero and reports how many values were clipped.
Units. Emission intensity comes in lb CO₂/kWh. Converting to kg CO₂/MWh multiplies by 453.59237, so a result that is off by a factor of about 450 signals a unit mix-up.
Changing categories. New energy-source columns, such as battery storage from 2025, change the set of fuels. Map every year to one consistent set before comparing years.
Average, not marginal. EIA’s CO₂ estimates use annual average emission factors, so hourly intensities built from these data are averages. My studies that used them state this boundary explicitly.
Totals. Hourly totals can differ from EIA’s monthly and annual publications because coverage and methods differ. Compare annual totals with EIA’s published figures as a check.

Used in. Emission-intensity-informed load regulation (GHG), with the ghg-load-regulation data pipeline; SMR cogeneration for a hyperscale data center, for hourly grid carbon intensity.


EIA-860, EIA-860M, EIA-861 and EIA-923
What it is. These are EIA’s core surveys of U.S. power plants and utilities: generators (EIA-860, annual, and EIA-860M, monthly), utilities and retail sales (EIA-861), and generation and fuel (EIA-923).
Coverage.

EIA-860. Generator-level data on existing, proposed and retired units at plants of 1 MW or more, organized as operable, proposed and retired-or-canceled tabs. Annual files cover 2001–2025; the final 2025 data were released on 10 September 2026.
EIA-860M. The monthly status of existing and proposed generators. Monthly files run from July 2015 to September 2026; the September file was released on 23 October 2026.
EIA-861. An annual census of U.S. electric utilities: retail sales, revenue and customers by state, sector and balancing authority, plus net metering, demand response, service territories and more. Data cover 1990–2025, with the final 2025 data released on 7 October 2026. A monthly companion, EIA-861M, also exists.
EIA-923. Monthly and annual generation, fuel consumption, fuel stocks, fuel receipts and costs, and environmental data. Data cover 2001–2026; the latest monthly release covers August 2026, and the final 2025 data were released on 14 September 2026.

Access. Download ZIP archives of Excel workbooks from each survey page. Many series are also on the EIA API.
License and terms. Public domain, as for EIA-930. Redistribution: allowed, with credit to EIA.
Known pitfalls.

Preliminary and final values. EIA-860M capacities are preliminary estimates that EIA later corrects without specific notice. Early-release annual data are not yet fully validated. Monthly EIA-923 releases cover only the plants in the monthly survey (about 3,000); the final annual file adds the plants that report annually.
Planned is not committed. EIA notes that capacities reported for planned units are not commitments by the facilities.
Retirements. The Retired tab of the annual EIA-860 is not comprehensive. The monthly inventory tracks retirements back to 2002.
Location and timing. EIA-860 gives each plant’s county and each generator’s operating month and year. My Texas framework uses the county to place market resources in zones, and the operating dates to count capacity only from the hour it entered service.
QA. Before using hourly inputs, compare annual energy by zone and technology with EIA-923.

Used in. TXH2: EIA-860 for locations, capacity and storage, and EIA-923 for QA. See the txh2-ercot-hydrogen data pipeline.


IEA Energy and AI
What it is. The International Energy Agency’s special report Energy and AI (10 April 2025), its follow-up Key Questions on Energy and AI (16 April 2026), and the online Energy and AI Observatory. A further IEA report, Powering Artificial Intelligence (14 October 2026), deals with integrating data centers into power systems.
Coverage. Global and regional estimates of data-center electricity consumption and installed capacity, with projections to 2030 and 2035. The 2025 report has a Base Case and three sensitivity cases: Lift-Off, Headwinds and High Efficiency. The Observatory (last updated 16 June 2025) shows installed capacity by data-center type (enterprise, colocation and hyperscale), capacity by region, and a map of large data-center hubs.
Access. Read the reports online or download the PDFs; the Observatory is interactive.
License and terms. The report pages carry a CC BY 4.0 licence. The IEA’s terms exclude standalone datasets, data explorers and data annexes from that licence and place them under its terms for non-CC material. Redistribution: report text and figures allowed with attribution under CC BY 4.0. Data from the Observatory are not CC BY; check the IEA’s terms or ask the IEA before republishing them.
Known pitfalls.

Modeled, not metered. The IEA notes that there are no comprehensive global statistics on data-center electricity use. Its figures come from its own model, so treat them as estimates.
Cases and editions. The cases diverge widely by 2035. Always name the case and the publication you cite, and check whether a later IEA publication has updated the figure.
Granularity. The figures are national and regional. They cannot stand in for utility, interconnection or nodal load data.
Recording. In my framework for the cost of delayed grid energization (CoDE), values drawn from capacity outlooks become scenario values, such as case sizes, and never observations. Each one is recorded in a provenance table with its source and access date.

Used in. Not used directly in my published studies. For the provenance rule, see the code-delayed-energization data pipeline.


SDWPF wind-farm SCADA dataset
What it is. SDWPF (Spatial Dynamic Wind Power Forecasting) is an open set of SCADA records from one wind farm of 134 turbines. It was released for the KDD Cup 2022 challenge and documented by its authors (Zhou et al.) in Scientific Data (2024).
Coverage. Records are at 10-minute resolution per turbine and include wind speed and direction, nacelle direction, blade pitch angles and active power. The full release, sdwpf_full, spans January 2020 to December 2021 (about 11.4 million records) with real timestamps, ERA5 weather variables and turbine elevations. The competition release, sdwpf_kddcup, holds the original 245-day file, which gives only a day index and time of day, with relative turbine positions.
Access. Download the CSV or Parquet files from figshare.
License and terms. The figshare record is licensed CC BY 4.0. Cite the Scientific Data article. Redistribution: allowed with attribution.
Known pitfalls.

Quality flags are defined but not applied. The dataset paper defines zero, missing, unknown and abnormal values. Power is unknown when it is at or below zero while wind speed exceeds 2.5 m/s, or when any pitch angle exceeds 89°; these cases often reflect curtailment or stops. The authors leave it to users to decide how to treat them.
Filter for your purpose. Forecast evaluation excludes those records. My multi-fidelity power-curve method keeps stops and curtailment on purpose, because its density-based sampling is meant to represent the turbines’ full operating behaviour. It removes only rows with missing or non-finite values and negative power, and reports how many rows each rule removed.
Time. In the 245-day file, a timestamp is built as (day − 1) days plus the time of day.
Units and sensors. Check power units against the 1.5 MW turbine rating. Nacelle anemometers sit behind the rotor, which affects the wind-speed readings. Look for duplicate intervals after merges and for long runs of stuck values.

Used in. Multi-fidelity Gaussian processes for wind power curves, with the mfgpr-wind-power-curve data pipeline.

title: Data & Tools for Energy-Systems Modeling
text:
Interconnection & planning

LBNL Queued Up
What it is. Queued Up is Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s annual compilation of U.S. interconnection queues, produced with GridTracker. Interconnection queues list the proposed generation and storage projects that have asked to connect to the transmission grid.
Coverage. The 2026 edition covers requests through the end of 2025. It includes all seven ISOs/RTOs and 50 non-ISO utilities, which together hold about 98% of installed U.S. generating capacity. The Excel data file (updated May 2026) contains the project-level dataset, a codebook and summary tabs; a PDF slide deck (June 2026) and interactive maps accompany it. The scope is generation and storage seeking transmission-level connection. Load requests, distribution-connected projects and behind-the-meter projects are not included.
Access. Download the data file and slide deck from the Queued Up page. No registration is required.
License and terms. The data file is licensed CC BY 4.0, and the page asks that it be attributed to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and GridTracker. Redistribution: allowed with that attribution.
Known pitfalls.

Requests are not plans. Most requested capacity is withdrawn. Berkeley Lab reports that of the capacity requested in 2000–2020, only 13% had reached commercial operation by the end of 2025. My Texas study treated queued capacity as an upper bound, at a 100% completion rate, and applied completion rates as scenarios in the model.
Selection. The framework filters for requests whose status is active and whose proposed in-service date falls on or before the target year. It sums their capacity by county, then by zone, and converts it to output with the zone capacity factors.
Power and energy. Storage requests are usually stated in MW. If a model needs MWh, convert with an explicit storage duration and record that assumption.
Not a load queue. Queued Up does not track large-load requests such as data centers. Utility and ISO large-load disclosures are separate sources.
Editions. Figures change from one edition to the next. Cite the edition and the date of the data file.

Used in. TXH2, via the txh2-ercot-hydrogen data pipeline.


ReEDS
What it is. The Regional Energy Deployment System (ReEDS) is NLR’s open-source capacity planning and dispatch model of the U.S. power system. Its inputs folder is a documented collection of planning data, covering load, supply curves, transmission, plant characteristics, fuel prices, financing and state policies.
Coverage. The contiguous United States, represented as 133 model balancing areas, over multi-decade planning horizons. The latest release, 2026.09.21, was published on 30 September 2026.
Access.

Clone github.com/ReEDS-Model/ReEDS. The earlier NatLabRockies/ReEDS-2.0 repository is archived.
Follow the documentation to set up the conda and Julia environments.
Large files, such as hourly demand and wind and solar profiles, are downloaded at run time from the hosts listed in inputs/remote_files.csv. Each input folder has a README that describes its sources.

License and terms. The code is BSD-3-Clause. ReEDS is written in Python, GAMS and Julia, and GAMS requires a commercial license; the documentation asks for a combined GAMS/CPLEX license. Small systems have been solved with an open-source solver, but the developers say that path is not actively maintained. The inputs are compiled from many sources. Redistribution: code allowed under BSD-3-Clause; for derived input data, check the terms of the original source first.
Known pitfalls.

Version pinning. Inputs change from release to release. Record the release tag and the identifiers of the remote files a run used.
Dollar years. The model documentation reports different inputs in different dollar years. Convert everything to one constant-dollar year before reusing it, as all my frameworks do.
Scope. Each balancing area is treated as a copper plate, and capacity decisions have limited foresight unless intertemporal mode is used. The results are least-cost planning outcomes under stated assumptions, not forecasts.

Used in. Not used directly in my published studies.


NRC and DOE advanced-reactor licensing resources
What it is. The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s public pages and records on licensing new and advanced reactors, and the Department of Energy’s Gateway for Accelerated Innovation in Nuclear (GAIN), which gives developers access to technical, regulatory and financial support.
Coverage.

Licensing pathways. Under 10 CFR Part 50, a plant needs a construction permit and then an operating license. Part 52 offers a combined license, early site permits and certified standard designs. The NRC’s licensing backgrounder explains both. Part 53, a technology-inclusive licensing framework based on risk insights, was published as a final rule on 30 March 2026 and took effect on 29 April 2026. It is optional; Parts 50 and 52 remain available. The NRC also lists proposed Part 57 requirements for microreactors.
Project status. The NRC publishes licensing dashboards for advanced-reactor applications under review. Its ADAMS public library holds more than three million documents released since November 1999.

Access. Everything is free. ADAMS has a public search, the dashboards are linked from the advanced-reactor page, and Federal Register notices are on govinfo.gov.
License and terms. The NRC’s site disclaimer treats its website as a U.S. Government work that is not subject to copyright and asks for credit when material is republished. Copyrighted third-party items on the site need the owner’s permission, and documents submitted by applicants may fall into that category. Redistribution: NRC-authored material allowed; check third-party documents first.
Known pitfalls.

Milestones are distinct. Acceptance of an application for review, completion of the safety and environmental reviews, the hearing, issuance of a construction permit, and authorization to operate are separate events. Under Part 52, operation is authorized only after the required inspections, tests and analyses are verified. Record which milestone a date refers to.
Cite the record. Use the ADAMS accession number (it starts with “ML”) or the Federal Register citation rather than a news report.
Pathway matters. The same design can be licensed under different parts of the regulations. Note the pathway when you compare schedules.

Used in. The smr-datacenter-cogeneration data pipeline lists public regulatory documents among the sources for reactor design parameters in the SMR cogeneration study.

title: Data & Tools for Energy-Systems Modeling
text:
Costs & technology

Annual Technology Baseline
What it is. NLR’s Annual Technology Baseline (ATB) is a yearly set of cost and performance estimates for electricity generation and storage technologies, with projections through 2050. A transportation ATB is published alongside it, and the electricity ATB pairs with NLR’s Standard Scenarios.
Coverage. The 2025 electricity edition was posted to the Open Energy Data Initiative (OEDI) in late August 2026. It covers capital cost, O&M, capacity factor, financial assumptions and levelized cost of energy by technology. Projections come in conservative, moderate and advanced versions, and there are separate financial cases, including an R&D-only case. The OEDI data lake holds the 2019–2025 editions.
Access. The data page links an Excel workbook, summary CSV and Parquet files on OEDI, Tableau workbooks, and the ATB-calc Python code. Read the disclaimer and the technical limitations first.
License and terms. The OEDI record is licensed CC BY 4.0. Cite the edition you use. Redistribution: allowed with attribution.
Known pitfalls.

Representative, not site-specific. The ATB leaves out site-specific resources, designs and regional labor and material costs. For a site-level cash flow, NLR points to SAM (see below).
Compare components. NLR’s guidance is that comparing capital cost, O&M and capacity factor directly is more reliable than comparing levelized costs.
Financial cases. The R&D-only projections reflect technology change alone, not short-term market swings, and separate cases include tax credits. Do not mix values from different cases.
Editions and errata. Values change between editions, and each edition has an errata page. My nuclear–data-center framework records the edition used, together with one constant-dollar year for every cost and price in a run.
Units. Convert each cost to the size unit the model uses (per kW of net output, per kWh of storage, or per kg/h of electrolyzer capacity) before use, not inside the model.

Used in. SMR cogeneration for a hyperscale data center (reactor, gas-plant and battery costs) and co-located solar and hydrogen (cost trajectories). See also the reopt-hydrogen-framework data pipeline.


Cambium
What it is. NLR’s Cambium datasets are modeled hourly projections of the U.S. electricity sector through 2050. They are built from ReEDS capacity-expansion runs and production-cost modeling for a range of futures, as a companion to the Standard Scenarios. Metrics include long-run and short-run marginal emission rates, average emission rates and several marginal-cost measures. The latest release, Cambium 2024, is the fifth annual edition, documented in an April 2025 report.
Coverage. Hourly data for a series of solve years from 2025 to 2050. The underlying models represent the contiguous United States as 133 balancing areas. Summary workbooks use 18 regions and include levelization tools.
Access. Download the full datasets from the Scenario Viewer (Cambium 2024 project, Download tab) and the summary workbooks from the NLR Data Catalog.
License and terms. The Data Catalog’s dataset license allows free use and copying, provided the full notice appears in every copy and publications credit DOE, the laboratory and its operator; their names may not be used for endorsement. The Scenario Viewer’s disclaimer likewise asks for credit and provides the data as is. Redistribution: catalog workbooks may be copied with the notice. For the full datasets I found no separate redistribution grant, so link to the viewer.
Known pitfalls.

Clock. The timestamp field is in Eastern Standard Time and timestamp_local in local standard time. Both are hour-beginning and ignore daylight saving. Every year has 8,760 hours and starts on a Sunday, and leap days are dropped. Market and EIA data are usually hour-ending in local or prevailing time, so shift before joining.
Purpose. NLR designs Cambium for long-term, forward-looking analysis, not for historical accounting or real-time decisions. For the 2020s, it suggests observed data instead.
Costs are not prices. Cambium’s marginal costs can differ from market prices and should not be used as retail rates.
Small changes only. The data carry no elasticities, so the values become less reliable the larger the intervention being analyzed.
Average or marginal. Choose the emission rate that fits the question. My load-regulation and nuclear–data-center studies used average intensities from historical EIA data and state that boundary.

Used in. Not used directly in my published studies.

title: Data & Tools for Energy-Systems Modeling
text:
Modeling tools

REopt
What it is. REopt is NLR’s techno-economic optimization platform for sizing and dispatching energy systems at buildings, campuses, communities and microgrids. It is available as a web tool, as an API, and as the open-source Julia package REopt.jl, which is the optimization engine behind both.
Coverage. One year of operation, at hourly or finer resolution, for PV, wind, storage, combined heat and power, conventional generation and electrification options. Resource profiles come from PVWatts and the Wind Toolkit, and utility tariffs from the Utility Rate Database.
Access. The API is at version 3; versions 1 and 2 were decommissioned on 31 March 2024. It needs a free key from developer.nlr.gov, limited by default to 1,000 requests per hour. To use REopt.jl, add the REopt, JuMP and HiGHS packages in Julia. An NLR developer key is needed to fetch PV and wind resource profiles, and a separate key to fetch utility rates.
License and terms. REopt.jl is licensed Apache-2.0. The web tool and API are free. Redistribution: code allowed under Apache-2.0.
Known pitfalls.

Series length. Every time series must have exactly 8,760 values per time step per hour, so drop 29 February in leap years. REopt.jl rejects a load series of the wrong length.
Calendar year. Set the load year to the year of your data so that tariff periods line up with weekdays. Built-in reference building profiles default to 2017, a year that starts on a Sunday.
Units. REopt works in kW and $/kWh, so convert market prices from $/MWh.
Keys. REopt.jl reads its keys from environment variables. Keep them there, never in scripts or repositories.
Extensions. When I started my wind–hydrogen studies, REopt had no electrolyzer, hydrogen tank or fuel cell. I added them, and the reopt-hydrogen-framework documents that formulation.

Used in. Co-located wind and hydrogen, co-located solar and hydrogen and offshore wind–hydrogen O&M, with the reopt-hydrogen-framework.


SAM and PySAM
What it is. The System Advisor Model (SAM) is NLR’s free desktop application for the performance and financial modeling of energy technologies such as PV, wind, concentrating solar power and storage. PySAM is its Python wrapper.
Coverage. Simulations of one year at hourly or subhourly time steps, driven by a weather file and coupled to financial models. NSRDB solar data can be downloaded from within SAM, and other weather sources are listed on SAM’s site.
Access. Download SAM for Windows, macOS or Linux. Install PySAM with pip install nlr-pysam. The package was renamed from nrel-pysam, whose last release is 7.1.1. PySAM 8.0.0 (July 2026) matches SAM 2026.7.3 and supports Python 3.9–3.14. The documentation is at nlr-pysam.readthedocs.io.
License and terms. SAM is free, and its open-source code is licensed BSD-3-Clause, as is PySAM. Redistribution: code allowed under BSD-3-Clause.
Known pitfalls.

Version match. Each PySAM release is built against a specific SAM version, and default inputs can change between versions. Pin the version and record it with your results.
Renamed package. Requirements files that pin nrel-pysam stay on the 7.x line.
Same year, same weather. My solar–hydrogen framework runs the SAM plant model with the same year and weather file as the rest of the inputs. It divides hourly thermal output and parasitic load by the plant’s design thermal output, so the optimizer can scale the plant.
One clock. Align SAM output to the model’s calendar year and time-zone convention before joining it to market prices.

Used in. Co-located solar and hydrogen, with the reopt-hydrogen-framework data pipeline.


HiGHS and linopy
What it is. HiGHS is an open-source solver for linear, mixed-integer and quadratic programs. It is a C++ library with interfaces for C, C#, Fortran, Julia and Python (highspy). linopy is a Python library, built on xarray, that writes linear, mixed-integer and quadratic models with labeled, N-dimensional variables and passes them to a solver.
Access. Install with pip install highspy; the current release is 1.15.1. Install linopy with pip, uv or conda-forge; the current release is 0.10.1. linopy does not work without a solver, so install at least one.
License and terms. HiGHS and linopy are both MIT-licensed. Commercial solvers that linopy can call, such as Gurobi or CPLEX, need their own licenses. Redistribution: allowed under MIT.
Known pitfalls.

MIP gap. The default relative MIP gap in HiGHS is 10⁻⁴. My frameworks set the gap explicitly (10⁻⁶) and document it.
Check the status. My frameworks stop with an error unless the solver reports an optimal solution, and some recompute the balance equations from the solution as a check.
Scale. Full-year, multi-zone or stochastic planning models can exceed what an open-source solver handles in practical time. The framework docs record where a commercial barrier solver was needed, and where a shorter horizon with hour weights served for screening.
Nonconvex terms. My supply-chain models use Pyomo with HiGHS. One bilinear variant needs a solver that handles nonconvex problems, so the framework offers an enumeration form that HiGHS can solve.

Used in. linopy with HiGHS: txh2-ercot-hydrogen, ghg-load-regulation, reopt-hydrogen-framework and smr-datacenter-cogeneration. Pyomo with HiGHS: supply-chain-microgrid-models.

title: Co-located wind and hydrogen energy systems
text:
ProjectsHydrogen systems





First author
253-MW wind farm, Texas8,760 hoursFour system configurationsMILP (REopt extension)Four ISO wind profiles


Research question
How do electrolyzers, hydrogen storage and fuel cells change the cost, curtailment and firm output of a grid-connected wind farm?


Key insight
A higher hydrogen price raised hydrogen's levelized cost but lowered system cost
As the hydrogen price rose, the optimizer built a larger electrolyzer to use more surplus wind. The larger unit ran at lower utilization, so each kilogram carried more capital and the levelized cost of hydrogen rose, while hydrogen revenue lowered total system cost. The cost per kilogram and the system's cost moved in opposite directions.


Why can a costlier kilogram mean a cheaper system?

A higher hydrogen price makes each kilogram worth more, so the optimizer builds a larger electrolyzer to capture more surplus wind. The extra capacity runs fewer full-load hours, so the cost per kilogram, the levelized cost of hydrogen, goes up. Yet the added hydrogen revenue lowers the net cost of the whole system. The cost per kilogram and the system's cost move in opposite directions.

Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study's data or results.




My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: I extended NREL's REopt optimization model with hydrogen components, ran the analysis and did the writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeNREL's REopt optimization model had no electrolyzer, hydrogen tank or fuel cell.What I didI extended REopt with these three components, with their costs, efficiencies, hydrogen sales and constraints, so it sizes and dispatches wind, battery and hydrogen equipment together.Why it matteredFour system configurations could then be compared in one mixed-integer model.
ChallengeA wind farm's value to the grid depends on firm output, not only on the energy it sells.What I didI set the model to deliver the largest stabilized output in every hour at the lowest life-cycle cost, and compared battery, hydrogen and hybrid storage on that basis.Why it matteredHybrid hydrogen and battery storage delivered the highest stabilized output of the four configurations.
ChallengeResults from one site and one weather year may not hold elsewhere, or as equipment costs fall.What I didI repeated the analysis with wind profiles from four ISO regions and with projected component costs to 2050.Why it matteredThe ERCOT site had the lowest costs but the highest curtailment, and falling costs led to larger electrolyzers and less curtailment.



Design choices

Fix the wind farm at its planned 253 MWAlternatives considered: optimizing wind capacity together with storageThe study asks how storage and hydrogen should be added to a planned farm near Snyder, Texas, so only those components are sized.



Method
Mixed-integer sizing and dispatch optimization for a 253-MW West Texas wind farm with ERCOT prices, with sensitivities to hydrogen price, region and future technology costs.


Key findings

In the Journal of Mechanical Design case study, adding an electrolyzer reduced total system cost by about 7%.
In the same study, using hydrogen storage with fuel cells reduced it by about 26% and sharply cut curtailment (the earlier TORQUE 2022 case reported about 9% and 30%).



Boundary conditions
Cost assumptions date from 2020–2023 and predate final federal hydrogen credit rules.


What it led to
I reused the extended model and added a concentrated-solar module to compare solar-hydrogen designs. Co-located solar and hydrogen plants

title: Hydrogen’s role in expanding renewable energy in Texas
text:
ProjectsHydrogen systems





First author
8 ERCOT weather zones8,760 hours9 scenariosTwo-stage stochastic LPInter-zonal hydrogen pipelines


Research question
Where should electrolyzers, hydrogen storage and fuel cells be built in ERCOT, and how should hydrogen move between zones, to absorb surplus renewable generation and supply industrial hydrogen demand under uncertain 2030 renewable build-out?


Key insight
Dearer gas power diverted green hydrogen to power generation and raised emissions
When gas-fired backup power became much more expensive, the model built fuel cells and turned stored green hydrogen back into electricity. Industry then drew more hydrogen from gas reformers, and the round trip from power to hydrogen and back lost energy, so total emissions rose although gas-plant emissions fell.


How can dearer gas power raise emissions?

When gas-fired backup power becomes more expensive, the model starts to use stored green hydrogen in fuel cells to make electricity in hours of low wind and sun. That hydrogen no longer supplies industry, so gas reformers fill the gap with fossil hydrogen. Converting electricity to hydrogen and back loses energy, so in the paper's high-price cases total emissions rose even though emissions from gas plants fell.

Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study's data or results.




My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: the data pipeline from public ERCOT market disclosures, the stochastic planning model, the analysis and the writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeThe model needed hourly wind and solar output for each of ERCOT's eight weather zones.What I didI built it from ERCOT's 60-day market disclosures: each wind and solar resource mapped to its county and zone, averaged to hours, gap-filled and summed, then turned into zone capacity factors.Why it matteredThe same capacity factors scaled planned capacity from the interconnection queue, so existing and future renewables shared one hourly basis.
ChallengeHow much planned renewable capacity is built by 2030, and how fast demand grows, are both uncertain.What I didI formulated a two-stage stochastic program: hydrogen equipment is sized once, then operated hour by hour in nine scenarios combining three completion rates and three demand levels.Why it matteredThe sizes minimize expected cost over all nine scenarios instead of fitting a single forecast.
ChallengeWind and solar output is concentrated far from electricity demand in the north and southeast, and from hydrogen demand on the Gulf Coast.What I didI added hydrogen pipelines between adjacent weather zones, with transport cost set by the distance between zone centres.Why it matteredThe model could then choose between making hydrogen near surplus power and moving it, or making it where it is used.



Design choices

Hold hydrogen demand fixed across scenariosAlternatives considered: treating hydrogen demand as a third uncertain factorReliable hydrogen-demand data were lacking and computational cost mattered; the paper names this as future work.
Move hydrogen only by pipeline between neighbouring zonesAlternatives considered: adding truck or rail transportPipelines are the relevant mode for large-scale, long-term deployment; other modes were left out to keep the focus on supply and demand uncertainty.



Method
Two-stage stochastic linear program. The first stage sizes electrolyzers, hydrogen tanks and fuel cells in each of ERCOT's eight weather zones; the second stage schedules batteries, electrolysis, fuel cells, gas-fired backup, reformer hydrogen and inter-zonal hydrogen transport hour by hour over a full year, in nine scenarios (three electricity-demand levels by three completion rates of planned renewable capacity). Inputs are built from ERCOT 60-day SCED disclosures, the LBNL interconnection queue and EIA data.


Key findings

Renewable (green) hydrogen covered only a few percent of industrial hydrogen demand; reformer hydrogen remained the main supply.
Modest load flexibility (±5%) reduced CO₂ emissions from combined-cycle gas generation.



Boundary conditions
Inputs reflect 2022–2023 conditions; post-2023 federal hydrogen credit rules are not modeled.


What it led to
Next I asked the same flexibility question of firm low-carbon supply: whether hydrogen production can make existing nuclear plants more flexible and profitable. Hydrogen integration and policy support for U.S. nuclear power plants

title: Small modular reactors for data centers
text:
ProjectsNuclear & data centers





Co-first author
Perspective articleTechno-economic sectionFOAK and NOAK costsReliability premiumLevelized cost of computing


Research question
What would it take for small modular reactors to power data centers, and which economic dimensions must a credible techno-economic assessment capture?


Key insight
Reliability requirements add a capital premium that levelized cost leaves out
A hyperscale campus needs Tier IV-level availability, so one reactor is not enough: with N+1 redundancy, a 300 MW campus may need 400 MW of SMR capacity. Standard levelized-cost estimates omit this reliability premium, so they understate the cost of firm on-site supply.


My contribution
Co-first author. Wrote the techno-economic analysis section, introduction and conclusions.


How I approached it

ChallengePublished SMR cost figures mix first-of-a-kind budgets with long-run nth-of-a-kind targets.What I didI set first-of-a-kind and nth-of-a-kind capital costs of SMR projects side by side and argued that assessments treat them as separate cases, each with its own financing and risk.Why it matteredLong-run figures make first projects look more viable than they are, and early data-center buyers carry that risk.
ChallengeLevelized cost of electricity leaves out cooling, which takes 30–40% of a hyperscale facility's energy.What I didIn the section I drafted, I proposed a service-based metric, the levelized cost of computing, which puts electricity and cooling costs over units of computing service.Why it matteredIt compares on-site nuclear, grid and renewable-plus-storage supply by what each delivers to the data center.



Method
Perspective synthesizing technology, economics and policy for SMR-powered data centers.


Key findings

Data-center reliability requirements add a substantial premium to the capital cost of on-site nuclear supply.
First-of-a-kind and nth-of-a-kind cost estimates for SMRs diverge widely, so assumptions must be explicit.
Service-based metrics, such as cost per unit of computing, and co-products such as heat matter for comparisons.



Boundary conditions
A Perspective: it frames the questions and evidence rather than presenting a new case-study model.


What it led to
Pricing the heat used for cooling, hour by hour, became the core of my boundary analysis for one data-center campus. Small modular reactor cogeneration for a hyperscale data center

title: Intelligent operation and maintenance in offshore wind–hydrogen systems
text:
ProjectsHydrogen systems





First author
Gulf of Mexico wind areaHouston refinery hydrogen demandMonte Carlo maintenance simulationTwo-stage optimization54 sensitivity scenarios


Research question
How much does prognostics-based operation and maintenance change the cost of an offshore wind farm supplying electrolytic hydrogen?


Key insight
A large maintenance saving became a small hydrogen-cost saving
Prognostics-based maintenance lowered wind operation-and-maintenance cost by about 10% and downtime by about 11%. The saving applies to the turbines alone, so its effect on the whole system was smaller: the levelized cost of hydrogen fell by about 2%.


My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: I linked an operation-and-maintenance simulation, developed with my co-authors, to the system techno-economic optimization, ran the analysis and did the writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeMaintenance strategy and system design were optimized in separate models.What I didI took the expected maintenance cost and turbine downtime from the maintenance optimization and used them as inputs to the system sizing and dispatch model.Why it matteredThis traced the effect of maintenance through to the levelized costs of hydrogen and electricity.
ChallengeAn offshore hydrogen plant needs a realistic site, buyer and price signal.What I didI placed the system in a federal Gulf of Mexico wind energy area, estimated Houston-area refinery hydrogen demand from the capacities of ten refineries, and used Houston load-zone prices.Why it matteredThis tied the case study to a designated site and an existing demand centre.



Design choices

Apply prognostics-based maintenance only to the wind turbinesAlternatives considered: applying it to the hydrogen equipment as wellCondition monitoring and prognostics are more mature for offshore wind than for hydrogen assets.



Method
Two-stage approach: Monte Carlo operation-and-maintenance simulation, then techno-economic optimization for a Gulf of Mexico site supplying Houston-area refineries.


Key findings

Prognostics-based maintenance lowered wind operation-and-maintenance cost by about 10% and downtime by about 11%.
At the system level, the levelized cost of hydrogen fell by about 2%.



Boundary conditions
Single site and one weather year; maintenance parameters from the collaborators' framework.


What it led to
These plant studies took the site as given; where hydrogen assets should go across a whole grid became the question of my Texas study. Hydrogen's role in expanding renewable energy in Texas

title: Hydrogen integration and policy support for U.S. nuclear power plants
text:
ProjectsHydrogen systems





First author
42 reactors7 ISO/RTO marketsHourly MILP dispatchLifetime cash-flow analysis2024 market prices


Research question
Can existing and new U.S. nuclear power plants improve their economics and operating flexibility by adding high-temperature electrolysis, hydrogen storage and batteries, and by selling energy, hydrogen and ancillary services?


Key insight
With the assumed hydrogen credit, hydrogen revenue can sustain an existing reactor but not pay for a new one
The study treats an existing reactor's capital as already spent, so revenue from power, hydrogen and reserves, with the assumed hydrogen credit, must cover running costs and the new equipment; most reactors studied then reached positive net present value. A new plant must also recover the reactor's capital cost, and new builds stayed below zero even with tax credits.


Why does hydrogen help an existing reactor more than a new one?

A reactor earns from electricity; with an electrolyzer it can also sell hydrogen and offer reserves, and a hydrogen production credit adds to that. The study treats an existing reactor's capital as already spent, so these revenues need to cover operating costs and the new equipment. A new plant must also recover the reactor's capital cost, and in the study the same revenues did not cover it.

Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study's data or results.




My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: the methodology, the optimization and lifetime techno-economic models (developed during my internship at Idaho National Laboratory), the analysis and the writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeSeven U.S. markets price energy and ancillary services differently, and each of 42 reactors faces its own prices.What I didI co-developed an hourly dispatch model that co-optimizes electricity sales, hydrogen production, storage and ancillary services under each market's products, run for every reactor.Why it matteredIt showed how market design, not only the reactor, shapes the value of flexibility.
ChallengeElectrolyzers and turbines are not ideal: efficiency varies with load, starts wear equipment, and ramping is limited.What I didI helped represent turbine and electrolyzer efficiency with piecewise-linear curves, track electrolyzer degradation from operation and start-ups, and enforce ramp limits and minimum stable load.Why it matteredFlexibility estimates then respect what the equipment can actually do.
ChallengeOne year of hourly dispatch had to become a lifetime investment case under several federal credits.What I didI co-developed a discounted cash-flow model with component-level capital costs, scheduled replacements and the 45U, 45V-type, 45Y and 48E credits, linked to the dispatch results.Why it matteredThe same operation could be judged as a retrofit (with and without 45U) or as a new build (no credit, 45Y or 48E); the hydrogen credit is assumed throughout.



Design choices

Take electricity and hydrogen prices as given (price-taking)Alternatives considered: equilibrium or game-theoretic market models with price feedbackThe study evaluates plant operation against observed 2024 prices; price feedback from wide adoption is stated as a limit and left to future work.



Method
Hourly mixed-integer optimization of turbine, electrolyzer and storage dispatch for 42 reactors in seven U.S. ISO/RTO markets using 2024 prices, linked to a lifetime cash-flow model with federal tax credits (45U, a 45V-type hydrogen credit, 45Y and 48E).


Key findings

Operated as baseload-only plants at 2024 market prices, nearly all reactors studied had negative net present value.
With hydrogen integration, including the assumed hydrogen production credit, a majority of the reactors reached positive net present value.
Integrated operation added output flexibility; ancillary-service revenue was a few percent of the total.
For new builds, investment and production tax credits substantially lowered the levelized cost of hydrogen.



Boundary conditions
Results rely on 2024 prices, price-taking market participation, modeled ancillary-service participation parameters, the assumed hydrogen credit ($3/kg for ten years) and a dispatch held fixed after the credit expires; price feedback from large-scale adoption is not modeled.


What it led to
New plants did not pay for themselves here, which raised the question of what could cover a new reactor's capital cost; AI data centers are the candidate buyer my next studies examine. Small modular reactor cogeneration for a hyperscale data center

title: Emission-intensity-informed load regulation for grid decarbonization
text:
ProjectsCarbon-aware grid





First author
12 U.S. grid regionsHourly EIA data, 2023Mixed-integer load regulationMonth, quarter, year windowsThree case studies


Research question
How much do the emissions attributed to electricity consumption fall when load is re-timed according to hourly average grid emission intensity across U.S. regions, and which strategies suit which types of grid?


Key insight
Shifting load toward cleaner hours cuts attributed emissions only modestly
Because total use in each window cannot fall, emissions drop only through the gap in intensity between hours, and the allowed range limits how much load can move. In the reported scenarios, reductions were on the order of one to two percent of regional totals or less, largest with longer windows and wider ranges in renewable-rich, diverse grids.


How much can re-timing load cut emissions?

Each hour of the grid has an average emission intensity. The model moves part of the load from high-intensity hours to low-intensity hours in the same window, within an allowed range, and keeps total use unchanged. Attributed emissions fall by the load moved times the intensity gap between those hours. Because the range is limited, the reduction is modest; it grows with a wider range and a longer window.

Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study's data or results.




My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: the methodology, data processing, optimization modeling, analysis and writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeGrid regions differ in renewable share, generation mix and intensity swings, so one strategy cannot fit all.What I didI helped group the regions by renewable penetration, generation diversity and intensity fluctuation, and tested one strategy dimension on each: window length, adjustment range and adjustment penalty.Why it matteredThis showed which strategies suit which types of grid, the question the study set out to answer.
ChallengeRe-timing load inconveniences users, which an emissions-only objective ignores.What I didI helped add a penalty on each adjusted hour, counted with a binary variable, and varied its weight.Why it matteredIt revealed that regions with low intensity fluctuation are more sensitive to the cost of regulating load.



Design choices

Re-time load without reducing total useAlternatives considered: also allowing demand reductionEmissions then fall only because load moves to cleaner hours, so the study isolates the value of timing.



Method
Mixed-integer load-regulation model solved for each optimization cycle (month, quarter or year): hourly load moves toward lower-intensity hours within an allowed adjustment range, without lowering the cycle's total consumption, and each adjusted hour carries a penalty. Applied to U.S. grid regions with EIA hourly data (2023), varying the cycle, the adjustment range and the penalty, and grouping regions by renewable penetration, generation diversity and intensity fluctuation.


Key findings

Longer optimization windows and wider adjustment ranges increase the reduction in attributed emissions, most in renewable-rich and diverse grids.
In the reported scenarios, reductions in attributed emissions are modest, on the order of one to two percent of regional totals or less.
Regions with low intensity fluctuation are more sensitive to the cost of regulating load.



Boundary conditions
Reductions are computed under average-emission-intensity accounting with perfect foresight; they are not estimates of the consequential (marginal) system response.

title: Supply chains with on-site microgrids and transactive energy
text:
ProjectsMicrogrids & supply chains





First author (AMM, SEGRE)
Multi-tier supply chainOn-site wind, solar, storageHourly grid buying and selling52 weeks of 168 hoursMixed-integer location model


Research question
Where should a manufacturing supply chain place its facilities, and how much on-site wind, solar and storage should each facility install when facilities can trade energy with the grid?


Key insight
With on-site renewables, wind and sun become part of the siting decision
When each facility can install its own wind, solar and storage and trade energy with the grid, a candidate site's renewable resource affects its operating cost. The model then weighs transport cost against resource quality, and storage became worthwhile under high peak prices or capped grid imports.


My contribution
First author of the location-allocation papers (AMM, SEGRE), for which I did most of the work. Second author of the JORS paper, for which I contributed to the optimization models and the case-study analyses.


How I approached it

ChallengeWhere a facility opens decides its wind and solar resource, while transport, production and energy costs depend on the same decisions.What I didWith my co-authors, I developed a mixed-integer model that opens factories and warehouses, routes products and sizes each open site's wind, solar and storage, with an hourly energy balance and grid trade.Why it matteredSolving these together showed that facility siting trades transport cost against renewable resource quality.
ChallengeWeekly store demand is uncertain, yet the network has to meet it reliably.What I didI modeled demand as a chance constraint with a set service level, written as its deterministic equivalent.Why it matteredThe model stays a mixed-integer linear program while holding the chance of a stock-out to the chosen level.



Method
JORS sizes on-site microgrids for fixed facility locations with production and inventory planning; AMM and SEGRE add facility location-allocation decisions.


Key findings

Facility siting trades transport cost against renewable resource quality (AMM).
On-site renewables lower total supply-chain cost under the modeled time-of-use tariffs.
In the AMM price scenarios, batteries became attractive at high peak electricity prices; in JORS, capping grid imports made storage worthwhile.



Boundary conditions
Stylized multi-echelon networks with synthetic distances and costs.

title: The cost of delayed grid energization for AI data centers
text:
ProjectsNuclear & data centers





First author
Present-value frameworkDeveloper, ratepayer, social ledgers300 MW-IT caseLatin hypercube screeningStaged service, bridge power


Research question
What does it cost when a large AI data center must wait for grid energization, and how does the delay affect the developer, electricity ratepayers and society?


Key insight
The cost of delayed grid energization depends on who is counting
A late grid connection costs the developer lost margin and carrying costs; ratepayers face utility carrying and stranding costs; society bears external costs. I keep these present-value accounts separate. In the study, a 36-month delay for a 300 MW-IT facility cost the developer on the order of $0.7 billion, while ratepayer exposure depended strongly on large-load tariff design.


My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: the framework, the model, the analysis and the writing.


How I approached it

ChallengeDelay costs fall on different parties, and a single total hides who pays.What I didI priced the delay in three separate present-value ledgers (developer, utility ratepayers and society) with a net-benefit test that states when they may be combined.Why it matteredAn acceleration option can then be judged against what it saves each party and what it costs.
ChallengeDelay costs of projects with different sizes and waits are hard to compare.What I didI defined two metrics: a delay cost intensity per MW-month, and a break-even acceleration payment for options that shorten the wait.Why it matteredThey make results comparable across project sizes, delays and mitigation options such as staged service or bridge power.
ChallengeInputs are uncertain, and the length of a delay and whether a project goes ahead may be linked.What I didI screened inputs with Latin hypercube sampling and rank correlations, and stress-tested the dependence between delay and realization and the large-load tariff.Why it matteredThe parameters are illustrative, so the study reports which inputs move the result, not a single forecast.



Design choices

Treat the delay as givenAlternatives considered: modeling the interconnection process that causes itThe framework prices the consequences of late service; why service is late, and network feasibility, are outside its scope.



Method
Present-value framework that converts delayed IT capacity into grid capacity requirements and prices the delay in separate developer, ratepayer and social ledgers, summarized by a delay cost intensity and a break-even acceleration payment; sensitivity and dependence stress tests.


Key findings

For a 300 MW-IT facility, a 36-month delay costs the developer on the order of $0.7 billion in present value.
Staged energization can recover a large share of that cost.
Ratepayer exposure depends strongly on large-load tariff design.



Boundary conditions
The delay is treated as exogenous and parameters are illustrative; network feasibility is not modeled, and the social perspective is illustrated with a single bridge-power example.

title: Small modular reactor cogeneration for a hyperscale data center
text:
ProjectsNuclear & data centers





First author
200 MWe data center, ERCOTBWRX-300 reactor8,760 hours109 scenario runsHourly MILP co-optimization


Research question
Under which reactor-capital, market and policy conditions can a small modular reactor colocated with a hyperscale data center, and using its steam to drive absorption cooling, supply the campus more cheaply than the grid?


Key insight
An output-based credit makes cooling with reactor steam more expensive
The Section 45Y credit is paid per megawatt-hour of electricity. Steam sent to the absorption chiller is steam the low-pressure turbine does not convert, so each unit of cooling heat gives up both power and the credit on it. The incentive that narrows the reactor's capital gap also raises the cost of recovering its heat.


Why does the credit discourage steam cooling?

Reactor steam can either drive the turbine or feed an absorption chiller that makes chilled water. The production tax credit pays only for electricity. Every unit of steam sent to the chiller lowers turbine output and forfeits the credit on that output. So a larger credit raises the price at which steam cooling pays, leaving more hours to the electric chiller.

Illustrative model with stylized numbers: it shows the mechanism described in the paper, not the study's data or results.




My contribution
First author. I did most of the work: I co-conceived the study, co-developed the methodology, wrote the model software, curated the data, ran the analysis, made the figures and wrote the original draft.


How I approached it

ChallengeThe value of steam cooling depends on hourly physics: wet-bulb derating, crystallization risk, part-load chiller efficiency and the turbine work lost to extraction.What I didI modeled absorption performance against hourly wet-bulb temperature with a crystallization cutoff, the electric chiller's part-load curve with SOS2 constraints, and extraction with a Willans-line penalty from a steam-table heat balance.Why it matteredPricing diverted steam matters: treating it as a free by-product can by itself decide the sign of a cogeneration result.
ChallengeOne-at-a-time sensitivities cannot show whether a project falls inside the region where colocation beats the grid.What I didI designed 109 scenario runs, a baseline and nine sensitivity groups, including a five-by-five grid of reactor and absorption-chiller capital costs and a grid of reactor capital by market year.Why it matteredThe joint grid placed grid parity near $5,000/kWe under 2023 prices and showed that chiller capital moves the margin by at most 13 points.
ChallengeOne BWRX-300 produces about 2.9 times the campus's average IT load, so the plant is partly a merchant generator.What I didI swept campus size from 0.5 to 3.0 times the IT load, with the reactor fixed and the grid connection enlarged only for campuses above the baseline size.Why it matteredSize matching explained part of the gap, not most: the cogeneration margin improved from −62% to −29% at three times the load.
ChallengeMargins measured against grid cost are distorted across market years, because the grid cost itself falls in low-price years.What I didI reported cross-year results also in absolute annualized cost, next to the grid-cost margin.Why it matteredIn absolute terms the market year moved the cogeneration cost by about $48 million a year, a fifth of the reactor-capital range.



Design choices

Extract steam at the high- to low-pressure turbine crossoverAlternatives considered: a parallel tap on main steamCrossover steam has already expanded through the high-pressure turbine, so it costs about half as much turbine work; a sweep of the penalty tests this assumption.
Keep a full-size electric chiller and let both chillers share dispatchAlternatives considered: absorption as the primary chiller, with electric backup for emergencies onlyThe absorber has no steam during refueling and runs mainly in high-price hours, so the optimizer chooses between the chillers hour by hour.
Levelize the ten-year 45Y credit over the 20-year comparison windowAlternatives considered: levelizing it over the reactor's 40-year lifeThis matches the credit to the annualized-cost comparison; the 40-year variant moves the thresholds but not the mechanism.



Method
Mixed-integer linear program that co-optimizes, for every hour of a year, reactor output, steam extraction at the turbine crossover, absorption and electric cooling, and grid exchange for a 200 MWe data center in Houston (ERCOT) colocated with a BWRX-300 reactor; grid supply and an on-site gas combined cycle are evaluated on the same hourly basis. 109 scenario runs vary reactor and chiller capital cost, market year (2022–2024), carbon price, cost of capital, cooling efficiency, battery storage and campus size, with the Section 45Y production tax credit as the baseline policy.


Key findings

At 2023 ERCOT prices and mid-range reactor capital cost (ATB 2024), the nuclear configurations cost 49–62% more than grid supply, even with the Section 45Y credit.
Grid parity at zero carbon price requires reactor capital near $5,000/kWe under 2023 prices. At nth-of-a-kind capital the nuclear options are 77–89% cheaper than grid supply in 2023, but between parity and 34% more expensive in the low-price 2024 market.
A carbon price of $53–64 per tonne of CO₂ closes the mid-range gap when exports are credited at the hourly average grid emission intensity.
Absorption cooling follows hourly electricity prices and supplies 38% of annual cooling, but adds $9.2 million per year relative to the reactor-only plant; it breaks even only at an installed chiller cost near $60/kWc ($570/kWc on a legacy-efficiency campus), against surveyed prices of $450–1,200/kWc.
Capital cost and policy set the boundary; operating choices move it far less. Across the tested ranges, reactor capital spans 321 percentage points of the grid-cost margin and the cost of capital 119, against 12, 13 and 1 for cooling efficiency, chiller capital and battery storage.



Boundary conditions
One colocation-style load profile at one Houston site; hourly average rather than marginal emission factors, with the carbon-price crossovers conditional on crediting exports; demand charges and ancillary-service revenues excluded; reliability not modeled on a common basis across options; the reactor is one fixed commercial unit. The numerical thresholds depend on these market, financing and crediting conventions; the mechanism does not.


What it led to
The same question also matters at the national scale, which is the subject of my next study. Data-center demand and the commercialization of small modular reactors

First author

Research question
Is concentrated solar power with thermal storage feeding high-temperature electrolysis more economic than photovoltaics feeding low-temperature electrolysis in West Texas?


Key insight
With cheap thermal storage, a variable-power electrolyzer gave the lowest hydrogen cost
Among the cases studied, concentrated solar power with thermal storage, running a high-temperature electrolyzer at variable power, gave the lowest levelized cost of hydrogen; holding the electrolyzer at constant power was the most expensive. The paper attributes the advantage of concentrated solar mainly to the low cost of thermal energy storage.


My contribution

How I approached it

Run the photovoltaic case without a batteryAlternatives considered: photovoltaics with battery storageA battery would not be cost-effective when hydrogen can be stored downstream, and low-temperature electrolyzers tolerate fluctuating input better than high-temperature ones.

Optimization of a 115-MW solar plant with electrolysis using SAM solar models, ERCOT prices and ATB cost trajectories.

Among the cases studied, concentrated solar power with thermal storage running the electrolyzer at variable power gave the lowest levelized hydrogen cost; constant-power operation was the most expensive.
